title: Rio2C: Latin America's Biggest Creativity Festival Bridges Borders
summary:
Rio2C, the largest creativity gathering in Latin America, is back for its seventh in-person edition from May 27 to 31 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Organizers expect to break last year's record attendance of 55,000 people and 2,088 speakers from 39 countries. But this year, the festival has a special mission: to bridge the gap between Brazil (the only Portuguese-speaking country in Latin America) and its Spanish-speaking neighbors.

Founder Rafael Lazarini says, 'We have particularly worked to break down the wall between Brazil and our Spanish-speaking neighbors, bringing creators and executives from Latin America. This 2026 edition consolidates Rio2C as the major gathering of the creative audiovisual industries of Latin American countries.'

The lineup is impressive. Argentine producer Axel Kuschevatzky, who worked on Oscar-winning films like 'The Secret in Their Eyes' and 'Argentina, 1985,' will speak about creative production. He says Rio2C is 'mind-blowing' because it covers music, video games, commercials, features, and TV all at once. 'Usually you have forums that are focused on one single thing. In Rio2C, there is such a wide array of different industries at the same time.'

Other notable speakers include Daniel Burman, head of original content for Disney+ Latam; Uruguayan musician Jorge Drexler, who won an Oscar for 'Al Otro Lado del Río'; and Adam Chase, an executive producer of 'Friends,' who will debate the limits of humor in the age of social media alongside Brazilian comedian Fábio Porchat. Javier Gómez Santander, a key writer on 'Money Heist,' will discuss creating high-tension narratives.

Rio2C is not just a conference—it's a hub for collaboration. Kuschevatzky notes, 'This is my third year in a row in Rio2C, and the last two times, I came back with projects.' With its focus on breaking down barriers, this year's festival promises to spark even more cross-border creativity.
why_it_matters: Rio2C shows how breaking language and cultural barriers can lead to exciting new collaborations, reminding us that creativity thrives when diverse voices come together—a lesson that applies to everything from music to video games. For Latin American teens, it means more stories from their region reaching global audiences.

background_read: Brazil is the largest country in Latin America and the only one where Portuguese is the official language, while neighboring nations like Argentina, Uruguay, and Chile speak Spanish. This language divide has sometimes made it harder for cultural industries to collaborate, even though they share many creative traditions.
Rio2C began over a decade ago as a film market and has grown into Latin America's most important creativity festival, spanning film, TV, music, advertising, and video games.

Prominent speakers this year include Argentine producer Axel Kuschevatzky (behind Oscar-winning films), Uruguayan musician Jorge Drexler (an Oscar winner for best original song), and Adam Chase (executive producer of the iconic TV show 'Friends').
The festival's goal is to become a central hub that unites the region's creative talent, overcoming historic communication barriers.

perspectives.description: The festival provides a platform for Latin American creators to connect, potentially leading to more regional projects and greater global visibility for their work. It helps artists find partners across language lines.

Some may worry that focusing too much on bridging Brazil with the rest of Latin America could overshadow the needs of other underrepresented groups or regions within Brazil itself. There's also a risk that commercial interests dominate over artistic experimentation.

Historically, Latin American cultural industries have been fragmented by language and politics; events like Rio2C are trying to overcome these structural divisions, much like how the European Union fosters cross-border film co-productions.

If successful, this edition could establish a lasting network that encourages bilingual collaborations, joint studios, and a stronger Latin American audiovisual market that competes globally. Future festivals might even include other non-Spanish-speaking Caribbean or indigenous creators.
